opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and it's really at the heart of a lot of the work my lab has been doing.

Off-the-shelf methods, things like SHAP, Integrated Gradients, saliency maps, were largely developed with fairly generic settings in mind: image classification, tabular data with a modest number of features that are roughly independent and individually meaningful. Biology breaks almost every one of those assumptions.

First, there's the issue of correlation. In gene expression data you have tens of thousands of genes, and they're highly correlated because they operate in pathways and co-regulated modules. When you apply a standard attribution method, the credit can get split arbitrarily among correlated genes, or concentrated on one gene that happens to be a slightly better proxy. So you get attributions that are unstable and hard to interpret biologically. You might run it twice with slightly different models and get a different "top gene," even though the underlying biology hasn't changed.

Second, the choice of baseline or reference distribution matters enormously, and it's rarely thought through. When you ask "why did the model predict this patient will respond to a drug," the explanation depends on what you're comparing against. Compared to an average patient? A healthy tissue sample? Patients of the same cancer subtype? Each choice answers a different scientific question. Generic tools tend to default to something like an all-zeros input or the training mean, which may not correspond to anything biologically meaningful.

Third, the unit of explanation is often wrong. Biologists usually don't care about a single CpG site or a single pixel in a histology slide. They care about pathways, cell types, tissue structures, higher-level concepts. So we've found you often need to either build explanations at the level of groups of features, or incorporate prior biological knowledge, so that the attributions line up with how scientists actually reason.

And finally, there's the question of what you want the explanation to do. In biology, the goal often isn't just to audit a model. It's scientific discovery: generating hypotheses about mechanisms, identifying drug targets, finding biomarkers. That raises the bar. You need explanations that are robust, that you can aggregate across many models or many samples, and that you can validate experimentally. For example, in some of our work on acute myeloid leukemia drug response, we found that explaining an ensemble of models and accounting for correlated features gave much more biologically coherent results than explaining a single model naively.

So it's not that methods like SHAP are wrong. They're principled, and we've built a lot on them. But treating them as a plug-and-play box you run after training is insufficient. You need to adapt them to the structure of biological data and to the specific scientific question you're asking. That's where a lot of the interesting research is right now.

r001.rationale: The response says genes are highly correlated because they work in pathways and co-regulated modules, and recommends group-level explanations to capture that biological structure rather than relying on individual gene attributions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks so much for having me, Sam. So I think the honest answer is that when we started applying explainable AI to biology, we quickly learned that the explanation itself is not the end goal. In most of the machine learning community, explainability is framed as a sort of debugging tool, right? You train a model, you want to know what it's doing, you run SHAP or integrated gradients or whatever, you look at a bar chart of feature importances, and you're done. But in biology, the explanation is really the starting point. The scientist wants to take those attributions and make a claim about the underlying biological mechanism, like which genes or which pathways are actually driving a drug response, or which molecular features are associated with a disease. And that's where off-the-shelf methods start to break down in a few important ways.

The first issue is that the features in biology are not independent. If you have, say, twenty thousand gene expression values as input, those genes are highly correlated, they sit in pathways, they regulate each other. Most attribution methods were really designed and evaluated on images or tabular data where you can sort of pretend each feature stands on its own. When you ignore that structure, the attributions get spread arbitrarily across correlated genes, and a biologist looking at that list will draw the wrong conclusion. So the explanation has to be aware of the biological structure, whether that's pathway membership, or gene regulatory networks, or the relationships between cell types.

The second issue is that we actually care about whether the explanation is faithful to reality, not just faithful to the model. A model can be ninety-five percent accurate and still be relying on something that's a technical artifact, a batch effect, the particular lab that generated the data. The attribution method will faithfully tell you the model is using that artifact, but it won't tell you that it's an artifact. So we've had to think about how to integrate prior biological knowledge, and also how to evaluate explanations against ground truth that comes from the biology itself, like perturbation experiments, CRISPR screens, things like that, rather than just against the model.

And then the third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is that the data in biology is often small, noisy, and high-dimensional at the same time. Many of the attribution methods have an implicit assumption that you can sample from a reasonable background distribution, or that the model is well-behaved off the data manifold. When you have a few hundred patients and tens of thousands of features, those assumptions just don't hold, and you can get explanations that are essentially fitting noise. So a lot of our work has been about developing methods where the explanations themselves are more robust and statistically principled, and where we can actually say something about uncertainty.

So to summarize, I'd say off-the-shelf methods are insufficient not because they're wrong in some mathematical sense, but because the scientific use case demands a kind of explanation that they were never designed to produce. We need explanations that respect biological structure, that can be validated against biological ground truth, and that are honest about uncertainty. And I think that's actually a really exciting direction, because when you get it right, the model stops being just a predictor and becomes a tool for discovery.

r001.rationale: The response says genes are correlated, belong to pathways, and regulate one another, so explanations must account for that biological structure rather than treat genes as standalone feature importance scores.

astra-6.text:
I think the key issue is that explaining a model’s prediction and answering a biological question are not necessarily the same thing. A feature attribution method might tell you which genes contributed to a prediction, but that doesn’t automatically tell you which genes drive the disease or what would happen if you intervened on them.

In biology, features are also highly dependent. Genes work together, and their expression can be correlated. So how you define a feature’s contribution—what you compare it against, and how you account for other features—really matters. Different choices can lead to different explanations, even for the same prediction.

So we need to start with the scientific question. Are we trying to understand the model, identify a biomarker, or generate a hypothesis about a mechanism? Then we need an explanation approach whose assumptions match that question, and a way to validate the findings. Feature attribution can be useful, but it isn’t, by itself, a biological explanation.

r001.rationale: The response says genes work together and can be correlated, and that individual feature contributions alone do not establish a biological explanation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the fundamental issue is that explaining a model’s prediction is not the same as explaining the biology. A feature attribution method might tell you that a particular gene was important for a prediction. But what does “important” mean? Does that gene provide information on its own, or only in combination with other genes? Is the model using a biological signal, or a technical artifact in the data?

This is especially challenging in biology because the features are highly dependent. Genes work together in pathways, and their measurements are often correlated. If you perturb one feature without accounting for those dependencies, you can create a combination that is biologically unrealistic. The resulting attribution can be misleading.

So we need to start with the scientific question and make sure the explanation method actually answers it. Understanding what a model learned, identifying a useful biomarker, and discovering a causal mechanism are different goals. Feature attribution can help, but an attribution score alone doesn’t establish a biological mechanism. That requires additional evidence and, ultimately, experimental validation.

r001.rationale: The response says genes work together in pathways and that individual feature attribution scores can be misleading when those dependencies are ignored.
